Q: Counting DISTINCT over multiple columns A:

When using SQL Server, (as this question is tagged for), your initially proposed subquery method is the most accurate way to count DISTINCT values over multiple fields.

SELECT COUNT(*) 
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT DocumentId, DocumentSessionId
    FROM DocumentOutputItems
) AS internalQuery

Many of the methods proposed in other answers either will not work in SQL Server or have edge cases which can result in incorrect counts.

Methods that do not work in SQL Server

COUNT(DISTINCT a, b))

This method works in some database types, but is not supported on SQL Server.

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT DocumentID, DocumentSessionID)
FROM DocumentOutputItems

Msg 102, Level 15, State 1, Line 1
Incorrect syntax near ','.

Suggested by spelunk1, APC, and Alexander Kjäll

COUNT(DISTINCT DocumentID || DocumentSessionID)

Concatenating fields with || is not supported in SQL Server. Additionally, in databases where this syntax is supported, it may incorrectly count consider some concatenations as non-distinct, such as 1|12 and 11|2 both being considered equal to 112.

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT DocumentID || DocumentSessionId) 
FROM DocumentOutputItems

Msg 102, Level 15, State 1, Line 1
Incorrect syntax near '|'.

Suggested by Jaanis Veinberg

Methods that may produce unreliable results

COUNT(DISTINCT(CONCAT(a, b))

This method can have incorrect counts depending on your field values. For example, the concatenations for 1|12 and 11|2 are not considered DISTINCT, as they both equal 112.

DocumentId DocumentSessionID
1 12
11 2 
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CONCAT(DocumentId, DocumentSessionId))
FROM DocumentOutputItems;

Result: 1

Suggested by spelunk1 and karmakaze

COUNT(DISTINCT CONCAT(a, '-', b))

While adding a column separator makes collisions less likely, they are still possible if your separator value is part of the data.

DocumentId DocumentSessionID
1 2-3
1-2 3 
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CONCAT(DocumentID, '-', DocumentSessionId))
FROM DocumentOutputItems

Result: 1

COUNT(DISTINCT CHECKSUM(a,b))

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CHECKSUM(DocumentId,DocumentSessionId))
FROM DocumentOutPutItems

According to Microsoft's documentation, there is a chance that two different values may give the same value for CHECKSUM.

If at least one of the values in the expression list changes, the list checksum will probably change. However, this is not guaranteed. Therefore, to detect whether values have changed, we recommend use of CHECKSUM only if your application can tolerate an occasional missed change.

For example:

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [#DocumentOutputItems];
CREATE TABLE [#DocumentOutputItems] (
    [DocumentId]    INT,
    [DocumentSessionID] INT
);

INSERT INTO [#DocumentOutputItems] ([DocumentId], [DocumentSessionID]) VALUES
    (3066, 77),
    (3062, 141);

SELECT
    DocumentId,
    DocumentSessionID,
    CHECKSUM(DocumentID, DocumentSessionId)
FROM #DocumentOutputItems
DocumentId DocumentSessionID CombinedChecksum
3066 77 49133
3062 141 49133

COUNT(DISTINCT (CHECKSUM(a,b)) + CHECKSUM(REVERSE(a),REVERSE(b)))

This method will fail with an overflow error if one of the field values contains a NULL.

DocumentId DocumentSessionID
1 null 
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT (CHECKSUM(DocumentId,DocumentSessionId)) + CHECKSUM(REVERSE(DocumentId),REVERSE(DocumentSessionId)))
FROM DocumentOutPutItems

Arithmetic overflow error converting expression to data type int.

Suggested by JayTee
